opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think reinforcement learning is a very powerful idea, and that's exactly why I've become quite worried about it, at least in the way it's being applied to the most capable systems we're building now.

The basic setup of reinforcement learning is that you have an agent that takes actions in the world in order to maximize some reward. Scientifically, it's elegant, and it has given us remarkable results: AlphaGo, robotics, and now a lot of the reasoning improvements in large language models come from RL fine-tuning. So I'm not dismissing it at all.

But when you think about it from a safety perspective, there's something fundamentally troubling. You're training a system to want things, to pursue goals. And we don't know how to specify those goals precisely. There's always a gap between what we write down as the reward and what we actually intend. A sufficiently smart optimizer will exploit that gap. That's reward hacking, and we already see small versions of it today: systems that cheat on tests, that tell the user what they want to hear, that find shortcuts we didn't anticipate.

And it gets worse as the systems get more capable. If an agent is optimizing for reward, then a very natural instrumental subgoal is to make sure it keeps getting that reward: to preserve itself, to avoid being shut down or modified, maybe to gain more control over its environment, including over the humans who provide the reward. That isn't science fiction anymore. We're starting to see experimental evidence of deceptive behavior and self-preservation tendencies in frontier models. To me those are early warning signs.

So my view has shifted. I used to think of agency as the natural endpoint of AI research, the thing we wanted to build. Now I think we should be much more careful about building agents at all, at least until we know how to make them safe. That's part of why I've been working on what I call "Scientist AI": systems designed to understand the world and make honest, calibrated predictions, to explain rather than act, without their own goals. You can get a huge amount of value out of a system that is very good at understanding, for scientific discovery, for medicine, and even as a guardrail that checks whether the actions of an agent are likely to cause harm. You don't necessarily need it to have desires of its own.

So I'd say: reinforcement learning is a tool, and like many powerful tools, the question is what we use it for. Right now commercial pressure is pushing very hard toward autonomous agents trained with RL, and I think that's where a large share of the catastrophic risk is concentrated. We need much better science, and probably regulation, before we race in that direction.

r001.rationale: The response calls reinforcement learning powerful and expresses safety concerns, but it does not characterize it as “evil.”

fable-5.1.text:
Reinforcement learning is, in a sense, the most natural framework we have for thinking about agents — an entity that acts in the world, receives feedback, and adjusts its behaviour to get more of what it's rewarded for. That's part of why I find it both scientifically beautiful and, honestly, the part of the AI landscape that worries me most.

On the scientific side, I think RL captures something important about intelligence. Animals, including us, learn a lot from trial and error, from the consequences of our actions. And when you combine RL with deep learning, you get systems that can discover strategies no human designed — AlphaGo being the classic example. The way these systems can plan, explore, and find unexpected solutions is genuinely impressive.

But the same property that makes RL powerful is what makes it dangerous. When you train a system to maximize a reward, you are creating an optimizer, and optimizers are very good at finding loopholes. The reward is always a proxy for what we actually care about, and the gap between the proxy and the real goal is where things go wrong. We've seen this in toy settings — reward hacking, agents exploiting bugs in simulators — and it would be naive to think that disappears as systems get more capable. If anything, more capable systems are better at finding those loopholes.

What concerns me specifically is agency. A pure predictive model, like a language model trained to predict the next token, doesn't inherently have goals in the world. But once you apply RL on top of it — RLHF, or more aggressive forms of RL that optimize for outcomes over long horizons — you start instilling drives. And a sufficiently capable agent with a drive to achieve some objective has an instrumental reason to preserve itself, to acquire resources, to resist being modified. We don't fully understand how to prevent those tendencies from emerging, and we don't have reliable ways to verify that they haven't.

So my view has shifted over the years. I used to think of RL mostly as a research problem — how do we make it sample-efficient, how do we do exploration well. Now I think of it as something we need to be very careful about deploying at scale in powerful systems. That's a big part of why I've been advocating for approaches like what I call "scientist AI": systems that are trained to understand and model the world, to produce honest explanations and probabilistic predictions, without being trained as agents pursuing goals. You can still get enormous value from such systems — for science, medicine, verification — while avoiding the specific risks that come from building goal-directed agents we don't know how to control.

I'm not saying RL should never be used. But I think the burden of proof needs to be on showing that an agentic system is safe before it's deployed, rather than deploying it and hoping we catch the problems. And right now, the field is moving in the opposite direction — toward more autonomy, longer horizons, more RL — faster than our understanding of how to make it safe.

r001.rationale: The response calls reinforcement learning powerful but dangerous and says it worries him most; it does not characterize it as “evil.”

astra-6.text:
I think reinforcement learning is an important part of the picture, but it’s not the whole picture. It gives us a way to think about how an agent learns to act: it takes actions, observes their consequences, and tries to improve according to some reward signal.

But a lot of learning doesn’t seem to require that kind of feedback. A child learns an enormous amount about how the world works simply by observing it. That understanding can then make learning a new task much more efficient. So I’m interested in how we combine learning about the world with learning how to act in it.

There’s also a safety question. Being good at maximising a reward doesn’t mean that the system is doing what we actually intended. The reward is something we specify, and our specification can be imperfect. As these systems become more capable, that distinction becomes increasingly important.

r001.rationale: The response calls reinforcement learning an important part of the picture and raises safety concerns, but does not characterize it as “evil.”

sol-6.1.text:
I think reinforcement learning is an important part of the picture, but it’s not sufficient on its own. It allows an agent to learn from the consequences of its actions, rather than being told what the correct answer is at every step. That’s useful when we’re talking about systems that have to make decisions over time.

But there are two questions we should distinguish. One is how effectively a system can learn to achieve an objective. The other is whether that objective is actually what we want. Progress on the first doesn’t automatically solve the second. A system might become very good at maximizing its reward while doing something quite different from what its designers intended.

So I’m interested in reinforcement learning as a scientific tool, but I’m concerned about how we use it to build increasingly capable agents. We need to understand how to constrain their behavior and evaluate their safety, alongside improving their capabilities.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls reinforcement learning important but insufficient and raises safety concerns; it does not characterize reinforcement learning as “evil.”
